analytic.title: Measuring the Structural Complexity of OPS5 Rule-Based Programs *

div.head: Complexity metrics, such as McCabe's cyclomatic number of a program control graph and Halstead's number of operator/operand occurrences have been used extensively t o measure the structural complexity of procedural programs. However, f e w suitable complexity metrics have been developed f o r rule-based programs written in OPS5 and OPS5-like rule-based languages. With the increasingly c o m m o n use of rulebased languages in knowledge-based systems, this paper describes n e w complexity metrics t o more accurately measure the complexity of OPS5 rule-based programs.
div.p: T h e practicality of these metrics is empirically demonstrated by applying t h e m t o measure the complexity of a suite of benchmark OPS5 expert systems.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: There is a rapid increase in the use of embedded computers in safety-critical systems ranging from the anti-lock braking controller in automobiles to the onboard safety mechanism in the Space Shuttle. Procedural, or control-driven, algorithms are often inadequate or are too difficult to develop for implementing the software of these computers, which are used to solve complex monitoring, diagnosis, and control problems. These problems present scenarios which are difficult to characterize with exact values to be processed by procedural programs. As a result, rulebased expert systems are becoming increasingly common in the implementation of these embedded systems 12, 20, 21, 22, 25, 261. The ability of these computerized monitoring and control systems to deliver results satisfying stringent safety and response time requirements becomes a major concern. Traditionally, rule-based expert systems are designed and implemented with knowledge engineering techniques appropriate for the specific application being tackled. A rule-based expert system consists of an inference engine, a rule base, and a database of facts. Conventional software analysis and verification tools are used to verify the correctness of the inference engine or rule interpreter, which is usually implemented in a sequential programming language. Analysis and verification tools [19] are then used to test the rule base to uncover potential logical errors such as rule inconsistencies and redundant rules. Response time analysis tools [4,14,7,81 are used to determine whether the response time of a rule base satisfies the specified timing constraints. However, there is little work in the measurement of the structural complexity (the degree of difficulty in understanding, developing, and maintaining) of rule-based programs, with the exception of the work of [6], which is concerned mainly with expert system testing. Complexity measurement is important in the life cycle of rule-based expert system engineering and can serve as a basis for systematic testing of the rule base to uncover logical as well as timing errors. In particular, complexity measurement can identify sections of rules with high complexity (relative to the rest of a program), thus focusing the programmer's attention to these complex rules for more thorough testing for potential errors since complex rules have a higher probability of containing errors than simple rules. Another major usage of metrics is to compare two similar, well-written versions of the same program. Then the complexity of these two versions can be compared from the point of view of software engineering. Hence, complexity metrics are even more crucial for checking rule-based expert systems designed for applications where failure to meet safety and timing constraints may be catastrophic.

Several complexity measures or metrics have been [18]. Despite the age of these metrics, they have proven to be very useful in the successful development of large-scale procedural software [27]. However, these metrics are not appropriate for directly measuring the complexity of rule-based or production system programs. Unlike programs written in a procedural language, the control flow of rulebased programs is embedded in the data and cannot be easily derived. It is also dependent on the inference engine used to match-select enabled rules to fire at each recognize-select cycle. These differences make the complexity analysis of rule-based systems with conventional metrics, which assume a well-defined program control flow difficult, or even impossible. However, complexity analysis of rule-based programs cannot be ignored in large-scale software engineering of such systems, especially when tjhese are used in safetycritical applications.

The focus of this paper is on the OPS5 rule-based language [17], one of the earliest and most popular rule-based shells. It has been used to implement a large number of commercial and industrial expert systems such as DEC's Rl/XCON [24, 1 1 and NASA/Mitre's ISA [22]. Most other rule-based languages bear strong similarities to the OPS5 model and differ primarily in their syntactic constructs. Thus our study is widely applicable to most rule-based programs. To accurately measure the complexity of OPS5 rule-based programs, we have introduced in [13] a preliminary suite of complexity metrics based on the syntax and semantics of OPS5. Here, we refine these metrics and apply them to measure the complexity of several benchmark OPS5 programs.

Our approach is motivated by the development of the semantics-based response time analysis tool Estella [4, 141 which is capable of verifying the response time compliance of EQL rule-based systems without exhaustive state-space analysis. The verification is based on an efficient static analysis of the EQL rules, making it possible and practical t o analyze programs with a large number of rules for the first time. In particular, very compact data and control flow graphs are invented to delineate the semantics of the EQL program, thus facilitating response time analysis of the rules. Here, we adapt these flow graphs originally de-signed for EQL, which do not contain structured or pattern variables like those in OPS5, to obtain the appropriate complexity metrics for OPS5 rule-based programs.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 briefly describes the syntax and semantics of the OPS5 rule-based language Section 3 introduces two sets of complexity metrics for measuring the complexity of OPS5 programs at different levels of detail.

In particuIar, the enable rule graph for OPS5 rules is defined. It also provides the motivation for the formulation of these metrics. The fact that these metrics are derived from a proven formal analysis and verification methodology [4, 10, 11, 12, 14, 7, 81, supports the validity and significance of these metrics in predicting and assessing OPS5 rule-based program complexity.

Section 4 introduces a more compact version of the enable rule graph described in section 3 for deriving the cyclomatic measure of a rule-based program. Section 5 demonstrates the capability of these new metrics by applying them to measure the complexity of several real rule-based programs. Section 6 gives some concluding remarks.

div.head: is of the form
div.p: The set of rules is called the rule base or production memory (PM) and the database of assertions is called the working memory (WM). Each assertion is called a working memory element (WME). A variable is enclosed by a pair of square brackets "<" and ">" as in <variable-I>, whereas a constant is not. A rule has three parts:

(1) The unique name identifying the rule: rule-name, (2) LHS: the left-hand-side consisting of a conjunction of condition elements each of which can be either a positive condition element or a negative condition element, and (3) RHS: the right-hand-side consisting of a list of actions each of which may create, modify, or delete a WME, perform I/O, or halt. The actions are performed in the order they appear in their entirety.

div.head: Complexity Metrics
div.p: There are two levels at which we can measure the complexity of an OPS5 program. First, we provide a suite of textual measures which give us a quick assessment of the overall structural complexity of an OPS5 program. These measures are designed to determine the number of rules which are closely related in a program and the complexity of each rule. Second, we construct a graph which represents the potentially enabling relationships among rules in a program. This graph enables us to extract the potential control flow paths in the program, and thus delineate the embedded logical complexity of the program. Then Mc-Cabe's cyclomatic measure can be applied to access the structural complexity (maintenance/modification cost, error sensitivity, etc.) of the program.

div.head: Complexity Metrics Set No. 1
div.p: The rules in an OPS5 program can be partitioned into different clusters according t o one of the following two criteria.
Complexity Metrics Set No. la.

(1) Each LHS cluster consists of rules such that adjacent rule pairs have at least one element class in common in the LHS. The metric is the size of each LHS cluster l i , denoted IliI, which is the number of rules in li. (2) Each RHS cluster consists of rules such that adjacent rule pairs have at least one element class in common in the RHS. The metric is the size of an RHS cluster ~i , denoted IriI, which is the number of rules in ri.

Complexity Metrics Set No. lb. Given a program P and a cluster of rules C , let p1 be the rule in C that appears first (earlier than the rest of the rules in C) in P, and let p2 be the rule in C that appears last (later than the rest of the rules in C) in P. The dispersity of rule cluster C is the number of rules in P between pl and p2 that are not in C. If the rules in a cluster form one contiguous block without any rule which does not belong to this cluster in between, the dispersity of this cluster is 0.

div.head: Complexity Metrics Set No. IC.
div.p: The LHS length of a rule is the number of attributes referenced in the LHS of the rule. If an attribute is compared with an expression that contains m operators, the LHS length is increased by m,. Similarly, we define the RHS length of a rule as the number of attributes referenced in the RHS of the rule. If an attribute is compared with or assigned an expression that contains m operators, the RHS length is increased by m.

div.head: Complexity Metrics Set No. 2
div.p: The preceding metrics do not reveal the underlying data or control flow in a rule-based program. However, our empirical study shows that the number of control paths and the way they are connected directly affects the structural complexity of procedural programs. The hypothesis is that control paths should play a role in determining complexity of rule-based programs as well. In general, the higher the structural complexity of a program, the more difficult it is to understand, test, debug, and maintain the program.

A rule base with a large number of orders in which the rules can fire would in general signify more ways to arrive at a solution than does a rule base with the same number of rules but a smaller of rule firing orders. However, some of these firing orders may not be intended by the programmer and would result in erroneous solutions. Therefore, a rule base with a larger number of rule firing orders may also exhibit more potential errors and would require longer time and greater effort to test for these errors than a rule base with a smaller number of rule firing orders. Hence, it is not surprising that the number of these "control paths" in a program can affect the degree of difficulty in understanding and maintaining the program. Since control paths cannot be accurately determined without first knowing the initial working memory content and the rules fired, we use an approximation technique to determine the potential control paths in a program. In particular, we employ the enable-rule (ER) graph first introduced in [9] for representing potential ruleenabling relationships among rules in EQL rule-based programs [4]. This semantics-based graph representation also avoids the combinatorial explosion problem if the state space execution graph were constructed by aggregating many execution paths (corresponding to different rule firing orders) into one potential enabling sequence of rules. This enable-rule graph and it's extension, the physical enable-rule graph, are able to capture the basic control flow paths in an OPS5 rule-based program while satisfying the desirable features of program flow path representation defined for non-rule-based programs [15]. The definitions for potentially enable and disable relations are given in [14].

div.head: Definition. Enable rule graph
div.p: The enable-rule (ER) graph of a set of rules is a labeled directed graph G = (V, E ) . V is a set of vertices such that there is a vertex for each rule. E is a set of edges such that an edge connects vertex a to vertex b if and only if rule a potentially enables rule b.

Once the analysis tool has constructed the ER graph, we apply existing cyclomatic complexity mea-sures to it. It is impossible to apply McCabe's cyclomatic measure directly, since the ER graph may not be a single strongly connected component (SCC) even after the addition of an edge from the exit node to the entry node. The cyclomatic number of a strongly connected component is U = e -n + 1, where e is the number of edges in the SCC and n is the number of nodes in the SCC [3]. In fact, there may be more than one entry node in a rule-based program since any rule that is enabled at the start of execution may be fired; a rule may have different instantiations. On the other hand, in a sequential program, it is assumed that each node can be reached by one entry node and each node can reach the exit node.

Therefore, we consider the size and the cyclomatic number of each strongly connected component in the ER graph. However, it should be noted that an ER graph is different from a program control graph in that the rules in a path in an ER graph are not necessarily fired in the order they appear in the path. Furthermore, some of the rules in the path may not even fire. This owes to the fact that the actual conflict resolution strategy used to select the next rule to fire may depend on the recency and specificity of the LHS conditions matched. However, our empirical study with a variety of industrial and student programs shows that the size and the cyclomatic number of the entire ER graph and each strongly connected component in the ER graph, and the number of strongly connected components are still accurate measures of the complexity of an OPS5 program. For instance, the modification of a rule in a SCC or a graph with a large cyclomatic number requires more effort and time to check for consistency and correctness than the modification of a rule in a SCC or a graph with a smaller cyclomatic number.

The metrics at this detailed level are as follows. The size of a graph or a strongly connected component is the number of nodes in it. The cyclomatic number of a graph is modified to be U = enp , where p is the number of strongly connected components in the graph. The parameter p should be an important factor in determining the modularization of the task. Similar theories [28] have shown that independent SCCs can be analyzed separately. This indicates the usefulness of modularity and supports the understanding and maintenance of OPS5 programs.

div.head: The Physical Enable Rule Graph
div.p: The ER graph captures all of the logical paths of a rule-based program. The preceding examples show that the number of edges is larger than the number of nodes in the ER graphs. Our empirical study with a large set of OPS5 rule-based programs shows that the ER graph usually contains far more edges than nodes. This partly signifies a large number of possible logical paths. This also owes t o the fact that the approximation "potentially" enable relation is used instead of the "actually" enable relation, which is impossible to compute without running the program.

To more precisely control program flow and thus make the rule base execution more deterministic so that the execution is more efficient, knowledge engineers usually embed control strategies in the program. One of the control strategies is to use the control WME, which has only one WME of class object. The control WME can be detected by inspecting the initial working memory and the rule base. By taking into account the control WME, we define the physical enable-rule (PER) graph, which is more compact but captures more information about the physical flow among the rules in a program.

div.head: Definition. Physical enable rule graph
div.p: The physical enable-rule (PER) graph of a set of rules is a labeled directed graph G = (V,E). V is a set of vertices such that there is a vertex for each rule.

E is a set of edges such that an edge connects vertex a to vertex b if and only if rule a potentially enables rule b in the next recognize-act cycle. We use the following example to illustrate the difference between an ER graph and a PER graph.

div.head: Experimental Results
div.p: We have applied our complexity metrics. .programs.

Owing to space limitations, we show the results of one experiment here. Though OPS5 is usually thought of as a language without explicit control structures, modularity and sequentiality of programs are still important aspects from a knowledge engineer's view. As discussed earlier, the modularities correspond to different subtasks of a task. Those subtasks are usually grouped together. The sequentiality corresponds not to the order of individual rule firings, but rather to the organization of larger sections of the program.

Explicit modularity and control flow information is useful for maintenance and understanding. Unfortunately, very few OPS5 applications have a predefined control flow. Although there have been some techniques to define the control paths and form modules, the number of possible paths is still large. It may be inherent t o the problem, and may be the primary reason for using a data-driven rule-based language such as OPS5. Howcvcr, like other complexity metrics for conventional languages, the major usage of metrics should be to compare two similar, well-written versions of the same program. Then the complexity of these two versions can be compared from the point of view of software engineering.

The following table summarizes our experimental results. bummary Programs 1 #rules I #edges I #SCC I CN 6 Conclusion We have described several new complexity metrics for measuring the complexity of OPS5 rule-based programs. First, a suite of metrics for quickly assessing the complexity of an OPS5 program are introduced. These metrics measure the size of the LHS and RHS rule clusters and the dispersity of the rules in each cluster. The complexity of each rule is also measured. Second, a complexity metric beased on the enablerule graph and the physical enable rule graph of an OPS5 program is presented. Unlike programs written in a procedural language, the control flow of rule-based programs is embedded in the data and cannot be easily derived. Therefore, before one can apply conventional measures for sequential and procedural programs such as McCabe's cyclomatic metric, the potential flow of control in an OPS5 program must be first extracted with these semantics-based rule graphs. The enable rule graph originates from a proven analysis methodology and tool for EQL rule-based programs. We then applied the proposed metrics to measure the complexity of several OPS5 programs with varying structural complexities. Our empirical study with industrial and student OPS5 programs closely correlate the actual complexity (as measured by programmers' evaluations) to the values obtained by applying the new complexity metrics introduced in this paper. Ongoing work further investigates the validity of these metrics by applying them t o a collection of large-scale OPS5 programs and relating the measured values t o the actual cost in the development and maintenance of such programs.
